output.population: 1,966,444 adults aged 18 years or older across 31 cohorts in 20 countries, excluding people with diabetes at baseline; 107,271 incident T2D cases.
output.exposure: Consumption of unprocessed red meat, processed meat, and poultry.
output.comparator: Lower consumption, modeled continuously within cohorts and pooled by random-effects meta-analysis.
output.effect: Higher consumption was associated with HR 1.10 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.15) per 100 g/day unprocessed red meat, HR 1.15 (1.11 to 1.20) per 50 g/day processed meat, and HR 1.08 (1.02 to 1.14) per 100 g/day poultry. Poultry findings were weaker under alternative modeling assumptions. Replacing processed meat with unprocessed red meat or poultry was associated with lower T2D incidence.
output.recommendation: The source interpretation highlights reducing meat consumption for public health and informing dietary guidelines; because the evidence derives from cohorts, these are association-based public-health implications rather than randomized causal effects.
output.applicability_boundary: Observational associations across multinational cohorts of adults without diabetes at baseline; confidence intervals were wide in some regions and poultry results were less robust to alternative modeling.
output.source_span: Greater consumption of each of the three types of meat was associated with increased incidence of type 2 diabetes

uncertainties: Observational cohort evidence cannot by itself establish causation.
Poultry associations were weaker under alternative modeling assumptions.
Confidence intervals were wide in regions outside North America, Europe, and the Western Pacific.
